titre: The Pilgrimage That Made the Price of Gold Fall in Cairo (1324)
accroche: Crossing Cairo on his way to Mecca, the emperor of Mali gives away so much gold that its value there stays low for twelve years.
contenu_vulgarise:
In July 1324, a caravan of several tens of thousands of people enters Cairo. At its head, Mansa Musa, ninth emperor of Mali, is making a pilgrimage to Mecca with, according to the chroniclers of the day, some 60,000 men, including a personal retinue of 12,000 slaves dressed in silk, and camels loaded with gold, as many as 80, each carrying nearly 140 kilograms, according to those same accounts. The empire of Mali then controls part of West Africa's gold mines, and its ruler stages the most spectacular display of it ever seen on the banks of the Nile.

## A Ruler Who Buys at Any Price

Musa stays three months in Cairo, from July to October 1324. He hands out gold to the poor in the streets, gives gifts to the emirs and dignitaries of the Mamluk court, and buys goods at the price the sellers name, without haggling. The effect is not long in coming: the influx of gold makes its value drop on the Cairo market. According to the chronicler Al-Umari, before Musa's arrival, a mithqal of gold was worth at least 25 silver dirhams; after his passage, it is worth only about 22 dirhams or less, and the market has still not fully regained its level twelve years later. Al-Umari himself never meets Musa: he visits Cairo more than a decade after the pilgrimage and gathers his account from Egyptian officials, such as Ibn Amir Hajib, who still remember the Malian ruler and speak of him, he writes, with admiration.

## A Fortune Less Precise Than the Figure Suggests

Mansa Musa's pilgrimage earned him the title, now repeated everywhere, of the richest man in history. Part of the shift is already there: today's historians point out that the figures given by the Arab chroniclers (60,000 men, 80 camels, a fortune put at billions of present-day dollars) belong to a rhetoric of wonder rather than to an inventory. None of these sources weighed the gold or counted the caravan; they report the impression left on witnesses already dazzled, years after the events.

But the figure that seems most solid, the drop in the price of gold reported by Al-Umari, also deserves to be put back in context. The historian Warren Schultz, a specialist in Mamluk monetary history, has shown that this price movement stayed within the ordinary range of fluctuations between gold and silver in Mamluk Egypt, and that it is only one disturbance among others in a market that was already volatile in this period: not the isolated, exceptional proof it is sometimes made out to be. Mansa Musa's passage did weigh on Cairo's prices; it did not, on its own, “ruin” them, as is sometimes repeated.

The episode thus shifts the real demonstration of power, but more modestly than is claimed: it is not the number of camels that proves the wealth of medieval Mali, nor even the scale of the price movement, but that a West African court could measurably weigh on the economy of one of the great trading centers of the Islamic world, in a chronicle kept by outside observers who had no reason to flatter it.

repere.texte: Before Mansa Musa's passage, the gold mithqal was worth at least 25 silver dirhams in Cairo; afterward it falls to about 22 dirhams or less, and the market has still not regained its level twelve years later.

carte.punch: One man crossed Cairo with so much gold that the price of gold stayed low there for twelve years.
carte.idee: In 1324, the emperor of Mali Mansa Musa gives away so much gold during his stay in Cairo that its value collapses on the local market, and does not recover for over a decade, according to the chronicler Al-Umari.

quiz.question: According to today's historians, what best allows us to gauge the wealth Mansa Musa displayed in Cairo in 1324?
choix: The exact number of camels reported by the Arab chroniclers
The lasting, documented drop in the price of gold on the Cairo market
The amount in present-day dollars calculated by twentieth-century historians
The number of mosques Musa is said to have had built during his stay
quiz.explication: The figures for the procession (men, camels) belong to a rhetoric of wonder, not an inventory, according to today's historians, and likewise the conversions into dollars, which are anachronistic. The drop in the price of gold reported by Al-Umari remains the most solid and measurable datum, even though the historian Warren Schultz has since qualified its scale, placing it within ordinary Mamluk market fluctuations rather than seeing an isolated shock; no mosque is mentioned in the sources on this particular stay.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long does Mansa Musa stay in Cairo in 1324, and what does he do during the stay?
choix: A week, long enough to meet the Mamluk emirs
A year, long enough to have a mosque built
Three months, giving gold to the poor and buying without haggling
A month, devoted solely to preparations for the departure for Mecca
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Musa stays three months in Cairo, from July to October 1324, handing out gold to the poor in the streets and buying goods at the stated price, never haggling.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the chronicler Al-Umari gather the account of Mansa Musa's passage through Cairo?
choix: By questioning Egyptian officials who still remembered Musa, more than a decade after his passage
By meeting Mansa Musa in person during his stay
By consulting the tax records kept by the Mamluk court
By accompanying the Malian caravan to Mecca
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Al-Umari never meets Musa: he visits Cairo more than a decade after the pilgrimage and gathers his account from Egyptian officials, such as Ibn Amir Hajib, who still remembered the Malian ruler.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the historian Warren Schultz show about the drop in the price of gold reported by Al-Umari?
choix: That it was invented out of whole cloth by Al-Umari to flatter the Mamluk court
That it actually doubled the value of gold instead of lowering it
That it affected only provinces far from Cairo, never the capital itself
That it stays within the ordinary range of gold/silver fluctuations in Mamluk Egypt, without being an isolated shock
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Warren Schultz shows that this price movement stayed within the normal range of fluctuations between gold and silver in Mamluk Egypt, one disturbance among others and not the isolated, exceptional proof it is sometimes made out to be.
